extracted.intended_audience: patent and trademark practitioners, counsel, and respondents in PTO/OED disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria governing Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) disciplinary investigations and charges before the U.S. PTO, including how statutes of limitations are triggered, what constitutes unauthorized practice of law before the Office, applicable definitions, burdens of proof, and related defenses. Useful for practitioners facing or advising on PTO disciplinary matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiation of disciplinary investigation / statute of limitations trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules require a “written submission from any source received by the OED Director” to initiate a disciplinary investigation and start the statute of limitations.  (37 C.F.R. § 11.1 is cited.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication (e.g., a state bulletin) does not constitute receipt by the OED Director and thus does not start the limitations period absent evidence the OED received the published notice.  The Tribunal also emphasized there was no evidence any written grievance regarding Respondent was received prior to the date in question, and mere public notice does not equal receipt by OED.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who constitutes receipt for limitations purposes (subordinate receipt / subdelegation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Receipt of a written submission by a subordinate within OED (e.g., a staff member) can trigger the statute of limitations; it is not necessary that the OED Director personally receive the grievance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a statute delegates authority to an agency, subdelegation to a subordinate is presumptively permissible absent contrary congressional intent (citing Ethicon Endo-Surgery, Inc. v. Covidien LP). The PTO's rulemaking language also treated initiation as when misconduct is reported to 'that section of the PTO charged with conducting section 32 proceedings,' indicating receipt by OED staff suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED tracking of statute of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the OED office, the OED Director keeps track of the statute of limitations based on the date the investigation is opened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should understand the Office tracks limitation periods from internal opening dates; requests for docketing statements may not change the governing rule that initiation is receipt by OED.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for establishing misconduct/defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings of misconduct in these proceedings are based on the evidence standard of clear and convincing evidence (the Tribunal found clear and convincing evidence that Respondent engaged in unauthorized practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defenses to allegations must be proven with appropriate evidence; mere argument or conspiracy theory without evidentiary support will not meet the necessary standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and prohibition of unauthorized practice of law before the PTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of that jurisdiction's regulation of the legal profession, or assist another in doing so; the PTO is treated as a 'jurisdiction' under the rule. Practice before the PTO includes rendering service, advice, and assistance in the presentation or prosecution of applications or other business before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of conduct constituting practice before the PTO include preparing/drafting responses to Office Actions that contain legal analysis and argument, acting as attorney of record, and submitting documents on behalf of a client. Prior decisions (e.g., In re Peirce, Jaeger) support treating these activities as the practice of law before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification to represent before the PTO (§11.14 and §11.1 definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only an individual qualified under §11.14 may represent an applicant, registrant, or party in non-patent (e.g., trademark) matters; an 'attorney' under §11.1 is an individual who is a member in good standing of the highest court of any State and not under an order suspending/disbarring/restricting practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A state suspension (e.g., administrative suspension by a state supreme court) means the individual is not an 'attorney' for PTO purposes during the suspension and thus may not represent others before the Office in trademark or other non-patent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client consent does not cure lack of authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a client is informed and consents to continued assistance, the client's consent does not authorize a practitioner to engage in the unauthorized practice of law when the practitioner is not qualified/authorized to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal expressly noted that obtaining a client's consent cannot transform an unauthorized actor into an authorized practitioner; consent is not 'tantamount to authorization to practice law.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/extraterritorial location does not negate PTO jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct performed outside the United States that is directed at or occurs before the U.S. PTO nevertheless constitutes practice before the PTO and is governed by PTO ethics rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal rejected the argument that Canadian residency during the suspension insulated the respondent from PTO rules; practice before the Office is defined by the Office-focused conduct, not the practitioner's physical location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of the rule is not a defense
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner's claimed lack of knowledge of PTO rules (e.g., duty to withdraw immediately upon suspension) does not excuse unauthorized practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision stresses that the rule is not 'arcane' for a practitioner with longstanding practice before the PTO, and mere ignorance would not negate clear evidence of drafting and participating in filings while suspended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice from PTO correspondence and continuing attorney-of-record status
rubrics_metrics.description: Continued receipt of PTO correspondence directed to the practitioner as attorney of record puts the practitioner on notice that the Office still considers them the attorney of record and triggers responsibilities to withdraw if not authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should ensure formal withdrawal and notification to the Office when no longer authorized; failing to do so while still being the listed attorney of record can support findings of unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brady disclosure rule not generally applicable to PTO disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Brady v. Maryland obligation to disclose exculpatory evidence does not generally apply to PTO administrative disciplinary proceedings; it applies beyond criminal prosecutions only in 'unusual cases' where consequences equal or exceed most criminal convictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal followed case law (Polidi and Fourth Circuit precedent) that Brady applies only when the defendant faces significant deprivation of liberty or the government's litigation tactics are particularly egregious. Absent such circumstances, Brady-based disclosure claims fail in PTO discipline contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law-of-the-case and preclusion of re-litigating prior rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: The law-of-the-case doctrine precludes revisiting prior rulings except in extraordinary circumstances such as an intervening change in controlling law, new significant evidence, or clear error causing manifest injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners cannot routinely reassert defenses previously stricken unless they can demonstrate one of the narrow exceptions; the Tribunal relied on this principle to bar re-raising already-decided defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective prosecution defense requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To succeed on a selective prosecution claim, a respondent must show both a discriminatory effect and a discriminatory intent in the federal prosecutorial policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal cited precedent stating the burden for selective prosecution is high; unsupported assertions or internet opinions do not constitute sufficient evidence of discriminatory intent or effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of searches and timeliness of exhibit production
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Tribunal orders the OED Director to search for and produce communications or records, a returning declaration that no relevant documents were found, combined with compliance with orders, will be credited absent contrary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late or untimely exhibits (e.g., untimely 'REX AUTH' exhibits) are unlikely to be admitted; bald assertions that a search was inadequate require evidentiary support. Allegations of concealment/spoliation must be supported by evidence rather than conjecture about redactions or missing text.
